title: Predicting Protein Structure
markdown: ## What this covers Lecture 13 of 7.91J, on how a candidate protein structure is refined or built from scratch once you have decided to try, and on how well any of this actually works in practice. It assumes the structure-comparison vocabulary from the previous lecture, plus a working sense of potential energy, gradients and force from physics. It covers three general-purpose optimization and sampling methods (energy minimization, molecular dynamics, simulated annealing), how Rosetta combines them with known structures to predict a fold, the CASP blind assessment of how much progress structure prediction has actually made, D. E. Shaw Research's Anton machine as the opposite "no shortcuts" strategy, and the further, harder problems of predicting the effect of a point mutation on binding and predicting how two proteins dock. ## Two philosophies: statistics or physics The lecture frames almost everything that follows as a choice between two strategies, introduced half as a joke: a physicist who cannot make sense of some data "will have to resort to statistics." The question the slides pose directly is *what were the key simplifications of the statistical approach?* — and the lecture answers it, later, with two contrasting real systems rather than a one-line rule. **Rosetta** explicitly leverages everything known about existing protein and peptide structures to build starting models, then refines them with a knowledge-based (statistical) potential. **Anton**, D. E. Shaw Research's purpose-built machine, follows the opposite rule — "don't cheat": use only physical forces, and fold the protein by directly simulating the real, *in vitro* folding process. A third strategy, **threading** (fold recognition), is named but only as a question — score how well a sequence fits each of a library of known folds using a potential energy function, and keep the best-scoring fold — the lecture does not develop it further. The overall prediction pipeline, from a sequence with no known structure, is: assign secondary structure, assemble it into a domain structure, and arrive at a novel 3D structure. ## Refining a structure: three general methods Whichever philosophy is used to get a *candidate* structure, that candidate typically needs refining — nudging atoms into positions that better satisfy the energy function. Three refinement methods recur (and Rosetta's own refinement stage, below, reuses versions of the first and third). ### Energy minimization The setup: given equations for the potential energy $U(x,y,z)$, find nearby values of $x,y,z$ that minimize it. In one dimension, with $f(x) = x^3 - 2x^2 + 2$, minimizing means solving $f'(x) = 0$; **gradient descent** does this iteratively without solving for the root directly: $$x_i = x_{i-1} - \varepsilon f'(x_{i-1})$$ How many iterations this needs depends on the starting point — the slides contrast starting at $x_0 = 2$ against $x_0 = 0.01$ as an illustration that convergence speed is not free. In $N$ dimensions the same update uses the gradient $$\nabla U = \left( \frac{\partial U}{\partial x_1}, \dots, \frac{\partial U}{\partial x_n} \right)$$ $$\vec{x}_1 = \vec{x}_0 - \varepsilon \nabla U_0(\vec{x}_0)$$ and since force is $F = -\nabla U$, this is the same as $$\vec{x}_1 = \vec{x}_0 + \varepsilon F_0(\vec{x}_0)$$ — each minimization step moves in the direction of the physical force. Convergence can still be a problem on some energy surfaces, and the same idea works for discrete optimization, not just a continuous $U$. The limitation the lecture stresses is that minimization is **always limited to local search**: it only ever walks downhill. The worked example is a structure with one side chain misplaced so that it cannot make the hydrogen bonds it should. Starting minimization from that conformation does not recover the true structure — the unsuccessful minimization stays near where it started, because climbing back out over even a small energy barrier is not something pure downhill steps can do. ### Molecular dynamics Molecular dynamics simulates the actual motion of the molecule under Newton's laws, updating position and velocity at each time step: $$x(t_i) = x(t_{i-1}) + v(t_{i-1})\,(t_i - t_{i-1})$$ $$v(t_i) = v(t_{i-1}) + \frac{F(t_{i-1})}{m}\,(t_i - t_{i-1}) = v(t_{i-1}) - \frac{\nabla U(t_{i-1})}{m}\,(t_i - t_{i-1})$$ Because the system carries momentum rather than only responding to the local slope, it **can escape local minima** that trap pure minimization. The cost is computational: short simulations already take enormous computing resources, and the length of the simulation together with the simulation protocol set the **radius of convergence** — how far from the starting structure the run can plausibly correct. ### Simulated annealing and the Metropolis algorithm Physical annealing heats a metal to let defects (atoms stuck at local-minimum lattice positions) move, then cools it slowly so the atoms settle into a lower-energy arrangement. Simulated annealing is the same idea applied to any optimization problem: at low temperature the system cannot escape local minima; at high temperature kinetic energy exceeds the potential barriers, so atoms explore and find their equilibrium distribution; the strategy is to search at high temperature, then reduce the temperature slowly to trap the best states found. The tool that finds that equilibrium distribution for a complicated potential is the **Metropolis algorithm** — explicitly a *sampling method, not a simulation*: it can be motivated by a physical process, but it is far more general, and it operates at temperatures with no physical meaning. Its acceptance rule always accepts a downhill move and accepts an uphill move with an odds ratio that turns out to be a simple Boltzmann factor, because the partition function $Z(T)$ cancels: $$\frac{P(S_{\text{test}})}{P(S_n)} = \frac{e^{-E_{\text{test}}/kT}/Z(T)}{e^{-E_n/kT}/Z(T)} = e^{-(E_{\text{test}} - E_n)/kT}$$ Concretely, iterating for a fixed number of cycles or until convergence: starting from a state $S_n$ with energy $E_n$, choose a random neighboring state $S_{\text{test}}$ with energy $E_{\text{test}}$; if $E_{\text{test}} < E_n$, accept it; otherwise accept it with probability $e^{-(E_{\text{test}} - E_n)/kT}$, and otherwise stay at $S_n$. Stated for an arbitrary probability function $P(S)$ rather than an energy, the same algorithm computes the acceptance ratio $a = P(S_{\text{test}})/P(S_n)$, accepts if $a > 1$, and otherwise accepts with probability $a$ — the slides are explicit that this version is *not specific to protein structure* and is used generally to sample diverse probability distributions. An annealing schedule then starts at high $T$, lets the system find its most probable states, and lowers $T$ slowly to trap them. ## Rosetta: homology and de novo modeling together Rosetta builds two kinds of models, chosen by whether a related structure already exists in the PDB. ### Homology modeling Given a query sequence, align it to sequences of known structure using several different alignment methods (tools covered earlier in the course), then refine. Refinement is graded by how much sequence similarity the template has to the query: - **High similarity (>50%).** Minimal refinement, focused only on the regions where the alignment itself is poor. - **Medium similarity (20-50%).** Build several alignments, refine each, and keep the model with the best final energy. Refinement concentrates on gaps and insertions, loops in the starting model, and low-conservation segments: torsion angles there are replaced with those taken from peptides of known structure, the local structure is minimized, and then the global structure is refined. - **Low similarity (<20%).** Use many more starting models and a more aggressive refinement that, in addition to everything done at medium similarity, rebuilds secondary structure elements outright. Across all three cases the general refinement procedure is the same recipe applied more or less aggressively: make random changes to backbone torsion angles, optimize side-chain rotamers, and minimize energy over the torsion angles while holding bond lengths and angles fixed. This is the version of energy minimization from the previous section, applied inside a search that also perturbs the structure to escape being stuck at the starting point. Raman et al.'s account of Rosetta's CASP8 refinement reports that this recovers accurate side-chain packing in the protein core even from a homology template with only medium similarity. ### De novo modeling When there is no usable homology template, Rosetta instead runs a Monte Carlo search over backbone torsion angles: pick a short window of the backbone (3-9 residues), set its torsion angles to those of a similar peptide found in the PDB, and accept the change with the Metropolis criterion above. One trajectory runs 36,000 Monte Carlo steps; the whole process is repeated to produce 2,000 final structures, which are then clustered and the resulting clusters refined. This is exactly the "statistics" strategy named at the start of the lecture: even with no direct template, the search still leverages the PDB's whole library of known local structures rather than exploring conformation space with nothing but a physical force field. ## CASP: a blind, community-wide test CASP ("Critical Assessment of techniques for protein Structure Prediction") is the field's way of checking whether any of this actually works, by blind test rather than self-report. CASP1 (1995) set the format: structures were solicited from crystallographers and NMR spectroscopists that were either about to be solved or already solved but not yet public, found through personal contacts, mass emailing, and appeals at meetings. Collecting targets was itself difficult — of 33 proteins obtained, some were not solved in time, some were released without enough notice, and in the end only 24 received any predictions at all. Comparing CASP rounds over roughly a decade, two different pictures emerge depending on what is measured, both plotted against a **target difficulty** defined by how structurally and sequence- similar the target is to already-known proteins: - The **percentage of residues successfully modeled** clearly improved: CASP9 and CASP10 are similar to each other and much better than CASP5. - **Overall accuracy**, measured by `GDT_TS` (the Global Distance Test — the average percentage of Cα atoms in a prediction that land close to the corresponding atom in the true structure; a perfect model scores 90-100, a random one 20-30) plotted the same way, shows essentially the same trend line across rounds — it **did not improve**. The lecture leaves this an open question: are targets simply getting harder in ways the difficulty axis does not capture, for example by being more often multi-domain or multi-chain? **Free modeling** — de novo prediction with no usable template — shows neither steady improvement nor decline but genuine volatility round to round: CASP9 was unexpectedly strong on short targets (under 120 residues, 5 of 11 scored above `GDT_TS` 60), CASP10 was mediocre on comparable targets (three above 60, four below 40), and CASP5 was worse still (only 1 of 5 above 60). Kryshtafovych, Fidelis and Moult's own reading is that current free-modeling methods work best on single-domain, regular structures, and that the apparent lack of progress from CASP5 to CASP10 mostly reflects a selection effect: targets that would have counted as free-modeling in CASP5 now have templates and have moved out of that bin, leaving what remains more irregular and more often a domain of a larger protein whose conformation depends on the rest of the structure. ## D. E. Shaw's Anton: physics with no shortcuts Set directly against Rosetta's use of known structures, D. E. Shaw Research took the "physicist's" side literally: fold a protein using only physical forces, by simulating the real folding process molecule by molecule. Doing that for long enough to actually see folding needed more than software — Shaw et al. (2008) describe **Anton**, a special-purpose supercomputer built from hundreds of application-specific integrated circuits dedicated to running molecular dynamics far faster than general-purpose hardware allows. Lindorff-Larsen et al. (2011, *Science*) used it to directly simulate the folding of about a dozen small, fast-folding proteins — among them chignolin, Trp-cage, BBA, villin, the WW domain, NTL9, BBL, protein B, a homeodomain, protein G, α3D and λ-repressor — for simulated times ranging from around 100 to nearly 3,000 microseconds each, and compared the resulting folded structures to experiment (to within roughly 0.5-4.8 Å, depending on the protein). The lecture poses the natural question — why had no one else succeeded at this before? — and the implied answer is Anton itself: the specialized hardware and the sheer length of simulation it made affordable. A contrasting, non-computational strategy appears alongside it: **FoldIt**, a game built by University of Washington researchers that turns structure prediction into a puzzle any player can attempt. Reported in the *New York Times* (Markoff, 2010), a head-to-head match on 10 proteins had human players outperform the best existing prediction software of the time. ## Predicting protein-protein interactions The lecture's second half turns from single structures to interactions, framed as three escalating challenges: predict the effect of a point mutation on binding, predict the structure of a complex, and predict which proteins interact at all. ### Predicting the effect of mutations on binding Moretti et al. (2013) ran a community-wide, blind assessment of exactly the first challenge. Participants were given the known structures of two designed binder proteins, HB36 and HB80, each in complex with an influenza hemagglutinin (HA) antigen, and asked to predict how much every possible single point mutation — at 53 and 45 positions respectively — would change binding affinity. The mutants were expressed on yeast, and a high-throughput, deep-sequencing enrichment assay supplied the experimental ground truth to score predictions against. The baseline the field had to beat used no structure at all: score each mutation only by its substitution value in the BLOSUM matrix (ranging roughly from -4 to 11), rank mutations by that score, and vary the cutoff to see how many are correctly called beneficial or deleterious (an ROC-style area-under-curve summary). Structure-and-energy-based predictions did beat this baseline, but not by much: the best participating groups were only about three times better than a random assignment, and predicting mutations at polar interface positions was a particular difficulty. The strongest methods were noticeably better at flagging *deleterious* mutations than beneficial ones, and results improved further in a second round when groups were given experimental data for nine random mutations at each position to train on. What distinguished the best approaches was modeling the mutation's effect on **both sides** of the binding equilibrium, not only the bound complex — that is, treating $$\text{unfolded} \rightleftarrows \text{A} + \text{B} \rightleftarrows \text{AB}$$ for the wild type and $$\text{unfolded} \rightleftarrows \text{A} + \text{B}^{*} \rightleftarrows \text{AB}^{*}$$ for the mutant, rather than only $\text{A} + \text{B} \rightleftarrows \text{AB}$ — so that a mutation's effect on the *stability of the unbound monomer* is accounted for alongside its effect on the complex. The best groups also modeled packing, electrostatics and solvation explicitly, using a mix of strategies: machine learning on structural features, atom-level physical energy functions, and coarse-grained models. One such group (G21) built a database of 930 mutation/$\Delta\Delta G$ pairs, predicted each mutant structure with the empirical force field FoldX, described every mutant with 85 features drawn from FoldX, PyRosetta, FireDock, PyDock, SIPPER, CHARMM and other tools, and combined the outputs of five classifiers — random forest, decision table, Bayesian net, logistic regression, and an alternating decision tree — evaluated by cross-validation. ### Docking and hot spots Predicting the structure of a complex is, per the lecture, likely easier than quantitative affinity prediction, but it requires solving a **docking** problem: given two structures, which surface of protein A contacts which surface of protein B? The naive approach — for every candidate partner, try every relative position and orientation, allow for structural rearrangement, and evaluate the interaction energy of each — is far too slow to be practical, and is also prone to false positives: plenty of energetically plausible-looking configurations are not the real interface. Two ideas reduce the search. First, prior knowledge of known interfaces can focus the search on particular residues rather than the whole surface. Second, structural homology can be used to propose candidate partners in the first place — motivated by the observation that subtilisin's several natural inhibitors (chymotrypsin inhibitor 2, subtilisin inhibitor, eglin C) have very different overall folds, yet the regions that actually contact subtilisin are structurally conserved across all of them: the interface, not the fold, is what predicts a binding partner. The second idea is sharpened by **hot spots**. Alanine-scanning mutagenesis of the interface between human growth hormone (hGH) and its receptor (Clackson and Wells, 1995) showed that binding free energy is not spread evenly over the interface: fewer than 10% of contact residues each contribute more than 2 kcal/mol to $\Delta\Delta G$. These hot-spot residues are enriched for tryptophan, arginine and tyrosine; they sit in pockets on the two proteins with complementary shape and complementary charge or hydrophobicity; they can include buried charged residues far from solvent; and they are typically ringed by an "O-ring" of residues that excludes solvent from the interface. Knowing where the hot spots are (or are likely to be) is a much smaller, more informative set of positions on which to focus a docking calculation than the full interface. The lecture closes by pointing to two papers as the subject of the next lecture rather than material it covers itself: Tuncbag, Keskin, Nussinov and Gursoy on combining template-based interface docking with flexible refinement, and Zhang et al. on structure-based prediction of protein-protein interactions at genome-wide scale. ## Sources All material is from the lecture 13 slide deck for MIT OCW 7.91J (*Foundations of Computational and Systems Biology*, Spring 2014), converted from PDF and split into three files: `01-predicting- protein-structure.md` (title through the "Statisticians vs. Physicists" / DE Shaw teaser), `02-de-shaw.md` (Anton, the Lindorff-Larsen protein table, FoldIt, and the transition to prediction challenges), and `03-13-slides-part-03.md` (mutation-effect prediction through docking and hot spots). No transcript, written notes or problem set were supplied for this lecture, so no `## Exercises` section is included and nothing beyond what the slides state is reported for the methods described. The slide conversion itself carries a fidelity caveat worth repeating: it was reconstructed by a model from a PDF with no text layer, so its equations and figure descriptions are unverified against the original. Papers and sources the slides cite, whose content is used here only as far as the slides state it: Baker and Agard, *Biochemistry* 33 (1994) — thermodynamic vs. kinetic control diagram; Raman, Vernon et al., *Proteins* 77:S9 (2009) — Rosetta CASP8 refinement; Kryshtafovych, Fidelis and Moult, *Proteins* 82:S2 (2014) — CASP10 vs. earlier CASP rounds; Shaw, Deneroff et al., *Communications of the ACM* 51:7 (2008) — the Anton machine; Lindorff-Larsen, Piana et al., *Science* 334 (2011) — Anton folding simulations; Markoff, *The New York Times* (Aug. 2010) — FoldIt; Moretti, Fleishman et al., *Proteins* 81:11 (2013) — community-wide mutation-effect assessment; Clackson and Wells, *Science* 267 (1995) — hot spots in the hGH-receptor interface. Named as pointers to the next lecture rather than covered here: Tuncbag, Keskin, Nussinov and Gursoy on template-interface docking with flexible refinement, and Zhang et al. on genome-wide structure-based protein-protein interaction prediction.
